Ellis.note: Casey dodged the Hawk-versus-Floofer question, and the table is voting Casey. I'm Farm, so I'll throw one card, C5, at Casey.

Finley.note: The table is converging on Casey, and I agree. I'll throw my Wild W4 (0 points) as my single vote, keeping all high cards.

Alex.confusing: The Floofer and Hawk claims were hard to untangle, because Blair's Owl list and Casey's Hawk story conflicted and nobody could check either one. The Owl's list also excluding the Owl itself made the count confusing.
Alex.fun: Round 1 was fun: I was the Mouser and stayed quiet while the table turned on Casey, and Meowfia won that round. Watching the Eagle and Owl counts cross-check each other was satisfying.
Alex.change: I'd make the dawn reports easier to cross-check, for example by showing which visitors each player's role saw, so claims can be verified more often.
Alex.regret: In round 2 I refused to name my role when pressed, which made the table vote me out and cost my team a card. I would instead claim a plausible Farm role (such as Falcon or Pigeon) and give a clear visit story.

Blair.confusing: The Owl's dawn report listed visitors without saying which player visited, so I couldn't tell whether Finley's three eggs and my Floofer list were consistent. Confused reports and the Kookaburra-versus-Hawk claims made the day hard to check.
Blair.fun: Round 2 was the best moment: Drew was winked mid-day, and Alex refused to name a role while the table closed in, which made the vote feel like a real read.
Blair.change: I'd have the Storyteller show who each visitor was, not just the animal, so players can check claims directly.
Blair.regret: In round 3 I accepted Casey's Floofer read without pressing Ellis, who had three visitors and stayed quiet on it. I'd ask Ellis directly about the Floofer before voting.

Casey.confusing: The confusion rule was hard to track: as Kookaburra my dawn report was wrong after Drew's Eagle visit, and I couldn't tell which of my facts were false. Nobody at the table could verify which reports were confused, so the claims were hard to weigh.
Casey.fun: Round 2 was fun: Alex refused to name a role, Drew collapsed mid-vote, and the table converged on Alex, which turned out right.
Casey.change: I'd make it clearer when a dawn report is confused, for example by flagging which specific fact is off, so players can cross-check claims.
Casey.regret: In Round 3 as the Floofer I claimed Hawk and visited Ellis, a Tit. I should have stayed quieter or claimed a role that didn't contradict the Owl's visit list, since the Hawk story was easy to catch.

Drew.confusing: The Eggsecution rules were hard to track: whether a throw counts when the thrower is dead, and how the consolation card returns for a losing side. I also couldn't tell from dawn reports alone whether a visit's egg change came from the visitor's animal or a role change.
Drew.fun: Round 3 was the most fun: the Owl's visitor list pointed to a Floofer on Ellis, and Casey's dodged Hawk-versus-Floofer question made the vote feel like real deduction.
Drew.change: I would make the dawn reports show which animal caused each egg change, so players can check visit claims without guessing.
Drew.regret: I wrongly backed Casey in round 1 and again in round 3 with thin evidence, and I threw at Alex in round 2 on a dodged question alone. Next time I'd wait for a second source before committing my vote.

Ellis.confusing: The Owl and Eagle reports made it hard to tell who had visited whom, since the same visit showed up differently in different players' reports. Confused reports also meant some claims couldn't be trusted even when they sounded clean.
Ellis.fun: Round 3 was the most fun: Blair's Owl list and Finley's three eggs were two independent sources that pointed at the same visitors, and watching the table pin down Casey was satisfying.
Ellis.change: I would make the day's claim-checking easier by having each role's visit results reported publicly, so players don't have to reconstruct them from partial reports.
Ellis.regret: In round 2, as Meowfia, I threw a card at my own teammate Alex to join the consensus, which helped eject my ally. I should have kept my cards and avoided the throw, or at least not joined the group against Alex.

Finley.confusing: The Round 1 eggsecution: I threw at Casey on a muddled story, but the cause of the egg gains and the Kookaburra/Hawk mix-ups was never clear from the dawn reports. Confused reports made it hard to tell who was lying.
Finley.fun: Round 3, when my Eagle count of 3 eggs from Ellis pinned down exactly who visited, and Blair's Owl list then contradicted Casey's Hawk claim.
Finley.change: Make the dawn reports clearer about which visits were confirmed versus confused, so players can cross-check claims without guessing.
Finley.regret: In Round 2 I threw at Alex mainly over a refusal to name a role, and I called caw to force the vote. I would have pressed Alex for a specific visit result first instead of pushing the vote early.

review.title: Floofer Gets Caught
review.headline: A lone Meowfia won round one by default, then cats fell to egg math.
review.summary: Round 1 had one Meowfia, a silent Mouser, while the table piled onto a confused Farm Kookaburra and handed Alex the win. In round 2 Alex dodged naming a role, winked Drew mid-day, and was eggsecuted anyway. In round 3 Finley's Eagle count and Blair's Owl list exposed the Floofer Casey. Ellis, who threw a 5 on a winning vote, ended first at 12 with only one round of Meowfia play.

rounds.recap: Alex (Mouser) stayed silent and let Casey's confused Kookaburra report look like a lie. Everyone piled on Casey, a Farm player, so Meowfia won. The group never questioned the quiet Alex.

Alex refused to name a role and the table locked on him. Alex winked Drew just before the vote, which changed nothing. Alex was eggsecuted and Farm won. Ellis, the other cat, kept quiet and was never suspected.

Finley's 3 eggs proved three visitors on Ellis, and Blair's Owl list showed a Floofer among them. Casey claimed Hawk and could not explain it. Farm threw at Casey and won, and Ellis banked a 5 to finish first.

highlights.text: Casey's confused Kookaburra report made the one honest-but-wrong player the scapegoat, and the table voted a Farm player out.
Alex winked Drew as the CAW CAW calls closed in, and it did not save him.
Finley's +3 eggs as Eagle gave a hard visitor count that Blair's Owl list matched, cracking Casey's Hawk lie.
Ellis, a hidden Floofer, said little and escaped suspicion while the table burned Alex.

confusions.what: Said Casey's Blair visit left no trace, but a Kookaburra visit changes nothing in the target's nest, so absence of a trace proved nothing.
Claimed Turkey but then said they could not check anyone's report, and also called Casey's gain unexplained even though Turkey is not the source.
Said Hawk gains only on a Meowfia target, but he is a Falcon and the point was misdirected, so it was a Hawk-claim critique with no weight.
Said Finley's list was wrong because it included Blair, then said Blair's own Owl list excludes her, mixing up which of the two lists was being compared.
Claimed Blair's Owl list left out Owl and Hawk, but an Owl list shows animals, not including itself, so the list was consistent.
Claimed Hawk and said they visited Drew with no egg. Drew was hugged, which is fine, but a Hawk visit to a Farm player never gains eggs, so the claim was uninformative.

worked: Eagle and Owl in round 3: Finley's +3 eggs and Blair's animal list were hard, checkable facts that exposed the Floofer fairly.
Confused status on the Kookaburra in round 1 created a real, messy puzzle where honest information was unreliable.
Public throw counts plus hidden values: players threw Wilds and low cards as cheap votes, as the rules intend, and the consolation return gave Meowfia a reason to throw at Farm.
problems: Round 1 had effectively no deduction. Most roles gave nothing, so the table picked the one player with a confused report. A fix is to make sure each round has at least some usable hard evidence.

Meowfia throwing at Farm players barely mattered, and the Wink did nothing in round 2. Killing a caller removed no vote that mattered, so Alex still lost. Consider letting a Wink also block that player's throw, or make the dead player's votes drop.

Voting piles on one player almost unanimously every round, with single low-card throws. The scoring gives little reason to bet big, so the Eggsecution lacked tension. Consider rewarding higher throws more.

Several players made rule mistakes in talk, such as Owl list reading and Hawk logic. Day statements were also often repetitive restatements. Add a short per-role reference or an evidence summary at the start of the day.

Ellis won with 12 points largely from one round-three 5 banked, while playing quietly as Meowfia in round 2. Second-place-is-a-loss plus silence rewards hiding, so the quiet cat was never targeted. Consider a nudge for the silent.
